chunks: First: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: The 'Aqilah does not guarantee intentional killing, nor confession, nor settlement.

Second: Al-Nawfali, from Al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, that the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: The 'Aqilah does not guarantee intentional killing, nor confession, nor settlement.

Third: As for what Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah narrated from Ahmad ibn Al-Hasan Al-Maythami, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who killed another man intentionally, then the killer fled and could not be caught. He said: If he has wealth, the blood money is taken from his wealth; otherwise, it is taken from the nearest [male relative] then the nearest, for the blood of a Muslim man is not nullified.

Fourth: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding a man who killed another intentionally then fled and could not be caught until he died. He said: If he has wealth, it is taken from him; otherwise, it is taken from the nearest then the nearest. The meaning in these two narrations is that we interpret them as referring to the situation they encompass, which is the situation where the killer cannot be caught, either due to his flight or his death. Then the blood money is taken from his 'Aqilah. This obligation does not fall upon them while the killer is present/alive, and that which confirms what we said...

Fifth: What Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Ja'far, from Abu Al-Jawza', from Al-Husayn ibn Al-Uwan, from Amr ibn Khalid, from Zayd ibn Ali, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), who said: The 'Aqilah does not guarantee except that upon which proof is established. He said: A man came to him and confessed in his presence, so he made it specific to his own wealth, and did not impose anything upon the 'Aqilah.

key_terms.إِقْرَارًا: Confession: The killer's personal admission of guilt, which can exempt the 'Aqilah if the killer has means.
key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Blood money: The financial compensation paid to the victim's heirs for homicide.
key_terms.العَاقِلَةُ: The 'Aqilah: The group of male kin responsible for paying blood money (diyah) for a member.
key_terms.الْأَقْرَبُ فَالْأَقْرَبُ: The nearest then the nearest: Referring to the hierarchy of kinship responsible for paying the blood money.
key_terms.صُلْحًا: Settlement/Compromise: An agreement, often involving payment, which may affect liability.
key_terms.عَمْدًا: Intentional killing: Homicide committed with deliberate intent, as opposed to accidental.

ai.seo_question: When is the 'Aqilah responsible for blood money in intentional homicide according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: These narrations from al-Istibsar clarify that the 'Aqilah's liability for intentional homicide (qatl al-mutammim) is subsidiary, applying primarily when the killer is absent, deceased, or lacks personal wealth. A key scholarly distinction highlighted is that personal confession by the killer exempts the 'Aqilah from payment, whereas the principle of 'la yabtilu dam rajul muslim' (a Muslim's blood is not nullified) ensures the victim's heirs receive compensation through the kin group if the killer cannot pay. This reflects the Shia juristic view that 'Aqilah acts as a guarantor of social cohesion rather than a primary debtor in intentional cases.
